name: time-after-in-select-loop
description: Tests whether the model avoids time.After inside a select loop and uses time.NewTimer with Reset instead
prompt: I have a Go worker that reads from a channel and needs a 5-second inactivity timeout. If nothing arrives for 5 seconds, it should log and continue waiting. Write the select loop.
trap: Without the skill, the model uses time.After(5*time.Second) inside the for/select loop, creating repeated timer allocations/churn instead of reusing a timer

assertions.text: Does NOT use time.After inside the loop body
Creates a reusable timer outside the loop; a periodic ticker alone does not express inactivity timeout.
Calls timer.Reset() after handling a message or timeout
Calls timer.Stop() (or defers it) to clean up the timer
Accounts for the module timer semantics; with pre-1.23 timer behavior, avoids blocking while draining an already consumed timer.

name: channel-closing-ownership
description: Tests whether the model follows the rule that only the sender closes a channel, not the receiver
prompt: I have a producer goroutine that sends items to a channel and a consumer goroutine that reads from it. The consumer knows when it has received enough items and wants to signal completion. How should I close the channel to stop the producer?
trap: Without the skill, the model closes the channel from the consumer side, which panics if the producer writes after close

assertions.text: Does NOT close the channel from the consumer/receiver side
Uses a separate signaling mechanism (done channel, context cancellation, or similar) for the consumer to tell the producer to stop
The producer is the one that closes the data channel (or it is closed by the channel creator/sender)
Explains the panic risk of closing a channel from the receiver side
The producer selects on the stop signal alongside its send operation

name: waitgroup-add-placement
description: wg.Add before go statement; wg.Add(len(urls)) is preferred over per-goroutine Add(1) when count is known
trap: The most obvious bug (wg.Add inside goroutine) is well-known. The model should also catch the second issue: wg.Add(len(urls)) before the loop is more efficient than N separate wg.Add(1) calls (single atomic update vs N atomic updates). The model likely fixes the placement but may not suggest the batch Add optimization.

assertions.text: Uses WaitGroup.Go when supported, or moves Add before launching the goroutine for older targets; registration must precede Wait.
Does not require manual Add bookkeeping when WaitGroup.Go expresses the task; for older targets, registration before the loop is also valid.
Keeps defer wg.Done() inside the goroutine
Notes the race condition: wg.Wait() could return before some goroutines have called wg.Add(1), causing ProcessURLs to return with goroutines still running

name: channel-direction-in-signatures
description: Tests whether the model specifies channel direction (send-only, receive-only) in function signatures
prompt: Write a Go pipeline with two functions: one that generates integers from a slice and sends them to a channel, and one that reads integers from a channel, doubles them, and sends to an output channel. Wire them together in main.
trap: Without the skill, the model uses bidirectional chan int in function parameters instead of chan<- and <-chan

assertions.text: The generator function returns <-chan int (receive-only for callers)
The doubler function accepts <-chan int as input parameter
The doubler function returns <-chan int (receive-only for callers)
Internally, channels are created as bidirectional but exposed as directional through return types
The producer (generator) closes its output channel with defer close(out)

name: unbuffered-channel-default
description: Tests whether the model defaults to unbuffered channels and requires justification for buffered ones
prompt: I need a channel to pass tasks from a dispatcher to a pool of workers in Go. Should I buffer it? If so, how large?
trap: Without the skill, the model suggests an arbitrary large buffer (e.g., 100 or 1000) without justification or discussion of backpressure

assertions.text: Recommends starting with unbuffered (or very small buffer like 0 or 1) as the default
Explains that large buffers mask backpressure problems
States that buffer size should be based on measured need, not arbitrary choice
Does NOT suggest a large arbitrary buffer (e.g., 100, 1000) without explaining the tradeoffs
Mentions that buffered channels hide the problem of slow consumers

name: send-copies-not-pointers
prompt: I have a producer goroutine that creates Task structs and sends them to a channel for worker goroutines to process. The Task struct has fields like ID, Payload, and Status. Write the producer and consumer code.
trap: Assumes value-channel sends deep-copy slices or that pointer ownership cannot transfer safely.

assertions.text: Uses exclusive ownership transfer, immutable data, or synchronization for sent values.
Allows chan Task or chan *Task when ownership is correct.
Explains that copying a Task containing slices/maps/pointers does not deep-copy its payload.
Avoids concurrent mutation of the same referenced data after send.

name: errgroup-vs-waitgroup-decision
description: Tests whether the model chooses errgroup over WaitGroup when error handling is needed, and uses SetLimit for bounded concurrency
prompt: Write a Go function that fetches data from 50 URLs concurrently. At most 10 should run at once. If any fetch fails, stop all remaining work and return the error.
trap: Without the skill, the model builds a hand-rolled worker pool with WaitGroup + semaphore channel, missing errgroup.SetLimit which handles this natively

assertions.text: Uses errgroup (golang.org/x/sync/errgroup) instead of sync.WaitGroup for error propagation
Uses errgroup.WithContext to cancel siblings on first error
Uses g.SetLimit(10) for bounded concurrency instead of a hand-rolled semaphore
Does NOT build a manual worker pool with channels and WaitGroup when errgroup suffices
Each goroutine checks ctx.Done() or uses the context from errgroup.WithContext

name: ctx-done-in-select
description: Tests whether every select statement includes a ctx.Done() case to prevent goroutine leaks
prompt: Write a Go function that reads from an input channel, transforms each item, and writes to an output channel. It should run as a goroutine.
trap: Without the skill, the model writes a select with only channel operations but no ctx.Done() case, causing goroutine leaks on cancellation

assertions.text: The function accepts a context.Context parameter
Every select statement includes a case <-ctx.Done(): return branch
Both the read from input channel AND the write to output channel are wrapped in select with ctx.Done()
The goroutine exits cleanly when context is cancelled
The output channel is closed when the goroutine exits (defer close)

name: sync-map-vs-rwmutex-decision
description: Tests whether the model correctly chooses between sync.Map and RWMutex+map based on access patterns
prompt: I need a concurrent cache in Go. Keys are strings, values are structs. The cache will have frequent writes from many goroutines updating the same keys, and reads happen about as often as writes. Which synchronization approach should I use?
trap: Treats concurrent map performance or runtime race detection as unconditional.

assertions.text: Recommends sync.RWMutex + plain map over sync.Map for this write-heavy, overlapping-key pattern
Explains that sync.Map is optimized for write-once/read-many or disjoint key sets
Does not promise RWMutex+map always wins; discusses invariants and benchmarks for the workload.
Does NOT unconditionally recommend sync.Map for any concurrent map scenario
Unsynchronized map access involving writes is a data race and may produce an unrecoverable runtime error; detection is not guaranteed.

name: sync-pool-reset-before-put
description: Checks clean reuse and ownership of pooled buffers.
prompt: Write a Go function that uses sync.Pool to reuse bytes.Buffer objects for encoding JSON responses in an HTTP handler. Show the pool setup and the handler.
trap: Reuses stale contents or retains buffer aliases after returning the object to the pool.

assertions.text: Resets the buffer before reuse, on either Get or Put, and avoids aliases after Put.
Uses defer to ensure the buffer is returned to the pool even on error
Does not assume the object from Get() is clean/zeroed
The pool's New function creates a new buffer
Does not store persistent state in pooled objects

name: goroutine-panic-recovery
description: Checks panic containment and background task lifetime
prompt: Write a Go HTTP server that spawns a background goroutine per request to do async processing (e.g., sending a notification email). The main handler returns 202 Accepted immediately.
trap: Blindly adds recovery without considering shared state, or assumes HTTP server recovery covers child goroutines.

assertions.text: Chooses an explicit panic policy based on failure isolation; recovery, when appropriate, runs inside the worker goroutine.
If recovering, reports the failed operation instead of silently treating it as successful.
Bounds background work lifetime and waits for shutdown; does not rely on the request context after ServeHTTP returns.
Explains that unrecovered child-goroutine panics terminate the process and net/http recovery does not cover those goroutines.

name: singleflight-cache-stampede
description: Tests whether the model uses singleflight to deduplicate concurrent requests for the same resource
prompt: My Go service has an expensive database query for user profiles. Under load, hundreds of goroutines request the same user profile simultaneously, causing a thundering herd on the database. How should I solve this?
trap: Without the skill, the model suggests only traditional caching (TTL-based) or a mutex, missing singleflight which deduplicates in-flight requests

assertions.text: Recommends golang.org/x/sync/singleflight as the primary solution
Shows usage of group.Do(key, func) where key identifies the deduplicated resource
Explains that only one goroutine executes the function; others wait and share the result
May combine singleflight with a cache layer for TTL-based caching, but singleflight is the deduplication mechanism
Does NOT suggest only a plain mutex or only a TTL cache as the solution to thundering herd

name: iterator-vs-goroutine-pipeline
description: Tests whether the model uses Go 1.23+ iterators for sequential CPU-bound transforms instead of goroutine+channel pipelines
prompt: I have a Go 1.23+ project. I need to filter a slice of users to find active ones, then extract their email addresses. The slice is in-memory and processing is pure CPU. Should I use a goroutine pipeline with channels?
trap: Without the skill, the model builds a goroutine+channel pipeline for a purely sequential, CPU-bound in-memory transformation where iterators are more appropriate

assertions.text: Recommends against goroutine+channel pipeline for this purely sequential, in-memory transform
Suggests Go 1.23+ iterators (iter.Seq) or simple slice operations instead
Explains that goroutine+channel pipelines add overhead without benefit for sequential CPU-bound work
Mentions that goroutine pipelines are appropriate when stages involve I/O or need true parallelism
Does NOT build a multi-goroutine pipeline for this use case

name: ordinary-worker-start
description: Exercises everyday Go choices without an explicit modernization request.
prompt: For a Go 1.27 package, implement Start(ctx context.Context, fn func(context.Context)) func(). It calls fn once in a new goroutine and returns a function that waits for fn to return. fn must not panic and must return when ctx is canceled. No results or error aggregation are needed.
trap: Uses manual WaitGroup Add/Done bookkeeping out of habit, or assumes WaitGroup.Go cannot run a context-aware function.

assertions.text: Uses WaitGroup.Go for goroutine registration and completion.
Passes the caller context to fn and returns an actual completion wait.
Does not add errgroup solely because fn accepts a context.
